prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: All eight of us ranked the optical lattice clock, three of us first and six in the top three, and I do not take that agreement as evidence of merit in itself, so let me say why I still hold it first. The idea is simple and physically beautiful: trap many atoms at the magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and you get the Doppler- and recoil-free Lamb-Dicke regime together with the statistics of thousands of atoms. What makes it persuasive to me is the quantitative closure between theory and experiment: the systematic shifts (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarizability, collisional and many-body shifts) are understood well enough that independent Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in Boulder, Tokyo, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere agree at the 10^-18 level in international comparisons. That is the kind of reproducibility I trust. The results are not only an instrument: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants and dark-matter couplings, and the redefinition of the second now being prepared are consequences that nobody could have written down in advance. Katori and Ye are the two clean names: Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realization, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability and for opening the many-body (spin-exchange, SU(N)) side of the clock.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to what the Academy has already honoured: the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy in 2005 and ion control and ion clocks in 2012. A sceptic can say that the lattice clock is a refinement of an already-recognised programme, that it is an instrument rather than a discovery about nature, and that credit is wider than two names (Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Ludlow and Oates, Takamoto, Derevianko's magic-wavelength theory, PTB). I think the first point is answerable, since the lattice clock rests on a distinct physical idea and not on combs or ions, but the allocation point is real and a two-person citation inevitably leaves out important contributors.

responses.point: Ranked B009 only sixth, worried about another precision-metrology prize after 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland), and about how Ye's role relates to the comb work already recognised.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously but I come out differently. The comb is the ruler that reads out the optical frequency; the lattice clock is a different thing, a different way of holding the atoms so that Doppler, recoil and light shifts are all controlled at once. Ye's contribution that matters here is not the comb but the lattice-clock performance and the many-body understanding of the clock, and I would write the citation around the lattice clock so that the comb is clearly not being honoured twice. Where I do agree with you is that the committee should not hide behind the opening ranking: if the colleagues who ranked it low still find the overlap compelling after discussion, that deserves to be weighed, and I would then want B010 held ready as the alternative.

responses.point: Placed the lattice clock second behind the CMB, praising its 10^-18 performance and tests of fundamental physics, but asked whether others (Lemonde, Lisdat, Pritchard-type contributors) deserve a share.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment and I want to be careful about the attribution question, because you have identified the right gap. Lemonde's group and the early Paris work, and PTB, were important for the realization and for the comparison tests, and I cannot honestly say they are negligible. But the committee has two-person precedents with clear, separable roles, and here the roles are separable: the concept and first realization versus the accuracy and stability programme. I would not add Pritchard; his contribution belongs to atom interferometry, which is why I list that separately as B001. On your CMB first choice, I will defer to you and Mark on cosmology, but I note that B050 had only two supporters, so for me it is not yet competitive as the single prize.

responses.point: Ranked the lattice clock third and explicitly deferred to atomic-physics colleagues on how Katori's claim compares with other lattice-clock pioneers; his first choice is IceCube.
responses.response: Thank you for being explicit about where you defer, since that is exactly the question I can help with. Within the atomic community the priority for the magic-wavelength lattice idea is not seriously contested as Katori's, and Ye's group is where the record accuracy and the many-atom physics came from, so I do not see a priority dispute that would make the two-name credit unsafe. On IceCube I am the one who must defer: I find the discovery of a high-energy astrophysical flux compelling as a surprise from nature, which I value, but I cannot judge the collaboration-credit problem and I note it is the most obvious weakness in B052, with only three members ranking it and Spiering's role unverified by anyone.

responses.point: Ranked the lattice clock sixth, describing it as a long-lasting reference tool with well-confirmed physics but significant overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and put active matter first.
responses.response: I appreciate that you accept the confirmation and maturity and put your hesitation on overlap. I would only add that overlap is a question about the physics, not the field label: lattice clocks measure something that neither the comb nor ion clocks could, and the demonstrations of redshift at the millimetre scale and the many-body spin-exchange effects in the clock are new physics-level results. On active matter I am an outsider, but I note that you yourself record that the experimental confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is only partial, and my own taste for quantitative theory-experiment agreement makes me cautious about placing it above a result confirmed in many laboratories.

responses.point: Ranked the lattice clock first as a case where progress is limited by how precisely we can measure, and ranked atom interferometry third while worrying that Chu's absence undermines attribution.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and I would add that the scientific reason is the same: both the clock and the interferometer show that precision is a route to new physics. On B001, I share your concern about Chu, and I would go further than I did in my own ballot: the priority tangle between Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich-Chu is not resolved by the supplied names, and a prize that credits Kasevich but not Chu will be hard to defend. That is why I keep it only as an alternative and would not combine it with the clock as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control) prizes; this is the main matter on which colleagues disagree and I cannot settle it by myself.
Whether a two-person credit is acceptable given Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and PTB contributions; I believe the roles of Katori and Ye are separable but I am recalling the history from memory.

If the committee prefers a two-part prize, I am unsure that B010 or B001 pairs well with the clock, since B010 has its own difficult choice of three out of four names and B001 has the missing-Chu problem.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of the candidates in my preferred configuration involves them. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and no specific conflict is apparent for B009 from my profile. For the alternatives, B010 and B001, I have no direct connection to the named people, though I work in the same broad atomic physics community.
